narrative:
The decision regarding your law school application was influenced by a prediction that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. This high probability indicates significant concerns about your preparedness for the exam, which ultimately led to the rejection of your application.

The most critical factors contributing to this prediction were your LSAT score, your academic performance in your third year, and your performance in your first year. Your LSAT score of 19 is notably lower than the average score of 37.18 among accepted students, suggesting that your test-taking skills may not align with the demands of law school. Additionally, your rankings in both your first and third years placed you in the lowest decile, while the average for accepted students was around the sixth decile. This indicates that your overall academic performance has not met the expectations typically seen in successful applicants.

These three features collectively pushed the prediction toward a higher likelihood of failure. Your lower LSAT score, combined with your low academic rankings, raised concerns about your ability to handle the rigorous coursework and testing required in law school and on the bar exam.

Moving forward, it would be beneficial for you to focus on improving your LSAT score and enhancing your academic performance. Consider seeking tutoring or preparatory courses to strengthen your skills. Additionally, gaining experience in legal settings through internships or volunteer work could provide valuable insights and bolster your application for future admissions.
